summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's penal code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries a maximum sentence of seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained at independence and carried into its first post-independence penal code, adopted in 2015, with an enhanced sentence.

The law is enforced against foreign nationals as well as residents. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, an Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government described him as a "dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country" and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local law including the penal code's prohibition. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one of them openly homosexual. Eritrea's ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the law prohibiting homosexual relations; Italian diplomats condemned the expulsions.

Detention facilities are used against people suspected of same-sex conduct. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, which is known for holding political prisoners and journalists.

Openly LGBTQI+ people risk imprisonment and for that reason did not take part in the political process, according to the US State Department's 2023 human rights report, which also records continuing societal discrimination. The same reporting found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity; LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship of LGBTQ issues is compounded by heavy social stigma, and in the early 2000s state-run radio and television broadcast programmes on the alleged dangers of homosexuality.

Official rhetoric is hostile. The government has labelled disloyal individuals "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles". It rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review recommendation to decriminalise same-sex sexual activity as "in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people", and has made no major effort to change or rescind the law.

No anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people, as the UK Foreign Office records; the UK raised the issue bilaterally and through the EU. The penal code makes no gender distinction for assault.

Criminalisation obstructs health and care access. ILGA and HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law on the ground that it makes prevention programmes directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an area of concern. No law bans conversion therapy; OutRight Action International found conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity widespread under social stigma, and LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.

Same-sex relationships have no legal recognition in Eritrea and same-sex couples cannot adopt. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law has no recognition route.
tangentialFactors:
Eritrea joined other African states in 2010 in rejecting the Yogyakarta Principles, the international statement of sexual orientation and gender identity standards.

Abuse, torture and beating of prisoners is described as commonplace in Eritrean detention, and some prisoners have been illegally executed, though the UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported that the death penalty was not used in 2013.
localsOnly:
Eritrean citizens are subject to the same prohibition within national institutions. Gay and lesbian people serving in the Eritrean military are reported to have been subjected to severe physical and verbal abuse and threats from superiors and fellow soldiers, on a 2002 account from a UK refugee claimant that remains unconfirmed.

Conversion therapy is offered to LGBTQ people in lieu of jail time, and no law prohibits the practice.

US State Department reporting on Eritrea records torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service alongside the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal stigma; national service obligations fall on citizens rather than visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources cite the offence both as Article 310(1) of the 2015 penal code and as Article 600 of the penal code; the relationship between the two numbering systems is not resolved here.

The 2002 account of abuse of gay and lesbian soldiers is unconfirmed.

No youth-specific care findings are recorded, and no data was identified on trans-specific violence, hate-crime enforcement, or screening and document-marker rules affecting trans travellers at Eritrean entry points.
